# When to bow out: the runtime interop pattern

Some Remotion compositions can't be translated cleanly. The skill should
recognize them upfront and recommend the **runtime interop pattern** from
[PR #214](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/pull/214) instead of
producing broken HTML.

## When to recommend interop

Run `scripts/lint_source.py` first. If it returns any blocker, recommend
interop. The blockers are:

| Rule                        | What it catches                                                |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `r2hf/use-state`            | useState driving animation                                     |
| `r2hf/use-reducer`          | useReducer driving animation                                   |
| `r2hf/use-effect-deps`      | useEffect/useLayoutEffect with non-empty deps (side effects)   |
| `r2hf/async-metadata`       | calculateMetadata returns a Promise                            |
| `r2hf/third-party-react-ui` | Imports from MUI, Chakra, Mantine, antd, shadcn, Radix, NextUI |

Each of these breaks the seek-driven, deterministic-frame model that HF
relies on. Translating them produces silently-wrong output.

## What the interop pattern actually does

Per [PR #214](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/pull/214), the
runtime adapter:

1. Bundles the user's Remotion code with React + `@remotion/player` via esbuild.
2. Mounts a Remotion `<Player>` inside an HF composition's HTML.
3. Pauses the player on mount.
4. Registers the player on `window.__hfRemotion` with `seekTo(frame)`,
   `pause()`, `durationInFrames`, `fps`.
5. HF's render loop seeks the player frame-by-frame via `seekTo(frame)`.

Result: Remotion's React tree renders at HF's deterministic frame ticks.
Custom hooks, useState, useEffect, MUI components — all work because
Remotion's React reconciler is doing the rendering.

## The recommendation message

When the skill detects a blocker, output something like:

> The Remotion source uses `useState` (and others), which can't be
> translated to HF's seek-driven HTML model. The recommended path is the
> **runtime interop pattern**: bundle your Remotion code with `@remotion/player`
> and let HF drive it frame-by-frame.
>
> See https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/pull/214 for the full
> implementation. Quick summary:
>
> 1. Bundle `entry.tsx` with esbuild: `npx esbuild entry.tsx --bundle --outfile=dist/bundle.js --format=iife --jsx=automatic`
> 2. Mount the Player and register on `window.__hfRemotion`:
>
>    ```tsx
>    const playerRef = useRef<PlayerRef>(null);
>    useEffect(() => {
>      playerRef.current?.pause();
>      window.__hfRemotion = window.__hfRemotion || [];
>      window.__hfRemotion.push({
>        seekTo: (f) => playerRef.current?.seekTo(f),
>        pause: () => playerRef.current?.pause(),
>        durationInFrames,
>        fps,
>      });
>    }, []);
>    ```
>
> 3. Reference the bundle from your HF `index.html` and render normally:
>    `<script src="dist/bundle.js"></script>`

## The lint output already includes recommendations

`lint_source.py` emits a `recommendation` field per finding. Surface those
verbatim — they're tuned per blocker rule:

```json
{
  "rule": "r2hf/use-state",
  "message": "useState detected — Remotion compositions that drive animation via React state are not deterministic frame-capture targets in HyperFrames",
  "recommendation": "Use the runtime interop pattern from PR #214 instead of attempting a translation"
}
```

## When NOT to bow out: warnings only

Some patterns produce warnings, not blockers — translate after dropping
the wrappers:

| Rule                      | Action                                                              |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `r2hf/lambda-import`      | drop the `@remotion/lambda` config; HF runs single-machine, log gap |
| `r2hf/delay-render`       | drop the call; HF handles asset readiness                           |
| `r2hf/use-callback`       | drop the wrapper, inline the function                               |
| `r2hf/use-memo`           | drop the wrapper, compute inline                                    |
| `r2hf/custom-hook` (pure) | inline the hook body if it's a derivation of `useCurrentFrame`      |
| `r2hf/static-file`        | replace `staticFile("x")` with `"assets/x"`                         |
| `r2hf/interpolate-colors` | translate to GSAP color tween (see [timing.md](timing.md))          |

These are documented in T4 cases 05–07.

`r2hf/lambda-import` is a warning — not a blocker — because Lambda
configuration is orthogonal to the rendered composition. Translating an
otherwise-clean Remotion comp shouldn't fail just because the author also
configured AWS Lambda for distributed rendering. The skill drops the
`@remotion/lambda` imports and `renderMediaOnLambda(...)` calls in step 3
(Generate) and writes a `TRANSLATION_NOTES.md` entry so the user knows to
set up HF rendering separately.

## When the source has BOTH blockers AND warnings

Bow out. The presence of a single blocker means the skill shouldn't
attempt translation — even if the rest of the composition is clean.
The user should use interop for the whole thing OR refactor the
blocker patterns out of their Remotion source first.

# Eval: how to validate a translation end-to-end

Every translation should be measured. The skill ships a source linter and
a tiered test corpus; the CLI's `diff` command scores the result. Together
they gate translation quality.

## The tools

| Tool                       | Input                       | Output                                                                        |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `scripts/lint_source.py`   | Remotion source dir or file | JSON findings + exit code (0 clean, 1 has blockers)                           |
| `npx hyperframes diff A B` | original MP4, HF MP4        | per-frame SSIM, worst cell per frame, cuts, `worst.jpg` sheet; exit 1 on fail |

Run them in this order: **lint → render → diff → (if fail) read the sheet**.

## Per-fixture flow

```bash
# 1. Lint the source — blockers mean stop
python3 ../../scripts/lint_source.py ./remotion-src/src/

# 2. Generate any binary assets (T2+T3 only)
[ -f setup.sh ] && ./setup.sh

# 3. Render Remotion baseline
cd remotion-src && npm install && npm run render
# -> remotion-src/out/baseline.mp4

# 4. Render HF translation
cd .. && node ../../../packages/cli/dist/cli.js render hf-src/ --output hf.mp4
# -> hf.mp4

# 5. SSIM diff, gated on the tier's mean threshold only
mkdir -p diff && node ../../../packages/cli/dist/cli.js diff ./remotion-src/out/baseline.mp4 ./hf.mp4 \
  --min-mean 0.95 --min-p05 0 --min-cell 0 --out ./diff --json > diff/summary.json
# -> diff/summary.json, diff/worst.jpg, diff/ssim.log
```

Before rendering, `npx hyperframes diff <baseline.mp4> hf-src --at 0.5,2,4.1`
scores the project at chosen times with no render.

## Reading `diff/summary.json`

```json
{
  "pass": true,
  "ssim": { "frames": 90, "mean": 0.974, "p05": 0.972, "min": 0.971, "cell_p05": 0.93 },
  "worst": [
    { "t": 1.2, "frame": 36, "ssim": 0.971, "cell": { "roi": [480, 270, 480, 270], "ssim": 0.88 } }
  ],
  "cuts": { "reference": [1.5], "yours": [1.5], "missing": [], "extra": [], "pass": true },
  "duration": { "reference": 3, "yours": 3, "pass": true },
  "sheet": "diff/worst.jpg"
}
```

| Field           | What it tells you                                                                |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ssim.mean`     | average SSIM across all frames; the headline number                              |
| `ssim.p05`      | 5th percentile: most frames sit above it                                         |
| `ssim.cell_p05` | each frame's worst cell of a 4x4 grid; a wrong element shows here, not in `mean` |
| `worst`         | the lowest-scoring moments, each with the cell (in original pixels) that failed  |
| `cuts`          | hard cuts on both sides; a missing or extra one is a sequencing problem          |
| `pass`          | every gate held: `--min-mean`, `--min-p05`, `--min-cell`, cuts and duration      |

## Threshold rule of thumb

Set the threshold ~0.02 below measured `p05`:

- Real translation regressions drop mean by 0.05+ — caught.
- Encoder/font drift between CI runs is bounded at ~0.01 — not caught.

If a calibration run's measured mean is far above your initial threshold
guess, _don't_ tighten the threshold to fit. Leave headroom — fixtures
re-rendered on different hardware will drift.

## When the diff fails

1. **Look at `diff/worst.jpg` first.** The worst moments side by side, each
   with its failing cell boxed, show whether the failure is structural
   (wrong scene durations, missing element) or cosmetic (different font
   weight, slight timing skew).
2. **Check `diff/ssim.log`.** Per-frame SSIM tells you _which_ frames
   failed. Cluster of bad frames in the middle of a scene = animation
   problem; bad frames at scene boundaries = sequencing problem.
3. **Re-read the relevant reference.** [timing.md](timing.md) for
   spring/easing issues, [sequencing.md](sequencing.md) for scene
   boundary issues, [media.md](media.md) for asset loading issues.

# Font translation Fonts are the dominant non-translation noise floor. Same `font-weight: 800` renders perceptibly bolder on HF's `chrome-headless-shell` than on Remotion's bundled Chromium when there's no real font installed. Validation showed this costs ~0.025 mean SSIM at the noise floor. ## Pattern: `@remotion/google-fonts/` ```tsx import { loadFont } from "@remotion/google-fonts/Inter"; loadFont("normal", { weights: ["400", "800"] }); ``` Translate to a `` tag in ``: ```html ``` Pull the family name and weights from the import path and `loadFont` arguments. HF's compiler inlines the Google Fonts CSS at render time, so you don't pay a network round-trip per render. ## Pattern: local fonts via `@font-face` ```tsx import { Font } from "remotion"; Font.loadFont("/MyFont.woff2", "MyFont"); ``` Translate to a `@font-face` rule: ```html ``` Copy the font file into `hf-src/assets/` next to the HTML. ## Pattern: system font fallback (no font load) ```tsx
...
``` Same string in HF — but be aware: on Linux without a real Helvetica installed (typical CI environment), Remotion and HF fall back to _different_ sans-serif system fonts because they bundle different Chromium versions. This is the noise floor: ~0.025 mean SSIM cost, visible as different stroke widths at large font weights (800+). If matching the Remotion render exactly matters for a specific fixture, load the same font explicitly — don't rely on system fallback. ## When in doubt: use Inter Inter renders identically across Chromium versions and is free. Translate any "system sans-serif" Remotion comp to Inter when you need to minimize font drift in the validation harness. ## Font loading and `delayRender` Remotion uses `delayRender()` to defer the first frame until fonts load. HF's compiler inlines Google Fonts at compile time and waits on `@font-face` readiness via the Frame Adapter pattern — the `delayRender` call drops in translation. See [media.md](media.md). ## Multi-weight loading When Remotion loads multiple weights: ```tsx loadFont("normal", { weights: ["400", "500", "700", "800"] }); ``` Inline all weights in the Google Fonts URL: ``` ?family=Inter:wght@400;500;700;800&display=swap ``` Translation rule: enumerate every distinct `font-weight` value that appears in the composition's CSS (`font-weight: 800` → weight 800 must be loaded). If the Remotion source loads weights that aren't actually used, drop them. ## Font subsetting Remotion's `loadFont` doesn't subset; HF's compiler doesn't either (yet). Don't try to optimize this in translation — it's lossless to keep the same weight set as the Remotion source.

The adapter auto-discovers animations registered on `window.__hfLottie` and seeks lottie-web via `goToAndStop` and current dotLottie players via `setFrame`. ## Pattern ```tsx import { Lottie } from "@remotion/lottie"; import animationData from "./hello.json"; export const MyComp = () => ( ); ``` Translates to: ```html
``` Key differences from a typical Lottie embed: - `autoplay: false` — HF drives playback by seeking - `loop: false` typically (unless Remotion's `loop={true}`) - `window.__hfLottie.push(anim)` is what hooks the animation into HF's per-frame seek ## Asset handling Remotion bundles the animation JSON via webpack import. HF needs the JSON on disk under `assets/` and references it via path: 1. Copy the animation JSON from the Remotion project into the HyperFrames project’s assets folder. 2. Pass that local path to `loadAnimation`, as shown in the example above. For dotlottie (binary) format, use the ESM build of `@lottiefiles/dotlottie-web`. Before rendering, copy `dist/index.js` and `dist/dotlottie-player.wasm` from the same pinned release into `hf-src/lib/dotlottie-web/`. Version 0.81.0 provides: - https://unpkg.com/@lottiefiles/dotlottie-web@0.81.0/dist/index.js - https://unpkg.com/@lottiefiles/dotlottie-web@0.81.0/dist/dotlottie-player.wasm The package's CommonJS entry cannot run as a classic browser script. Set the local WASM URL before constructing the player; the render then loads the SDK, WASM and animation from project files. ```html ``` The HF adapter supports `goToAndStop` for lottie-web, `setFrame` for current dotLottie players, and `setCurrentRawFrameValue` / `seek` for older player shapes. ## Multiple Lottie animations Multiple `` instances in one composition work — push each one onto `window.__hfLottie` and the adapter will seek all of them in sync: ```js window.__hfLottie.push(anim1); window.__hfLottie.push(anim2); window.__hfLottie.push(anim3); ``` ## Lottie source isn't actually translation-blocking Lottie animations encode their own deterministic timeline. They're the _easiest_ part of a Remotion composition to translate because the animation logic is already self-contained — neither Remotion nor HF "animate" them, both just seek them. Translation cost is near-zero. ## After Effects → Lottie limitations Lottie supports a subset of After Effects features. Expressions, most Effects (drop shadow, color overlay), all blend modes beyond Normal/Add/ Multiply, luma mattes, and most 3D parameters are not supported. If the Remotion composition uses a Lottie file that depends on these, the animation will break in BOTH Remotion and HF — this isn't a translation problem, it's a Lottie limitation. See [airbnb/lottie/after-effects.md](https://github.com/airbnb/lottie/blob/master/after-effects.md) for the full supported feature list. ## Loop behavior Remotion's `loop={true}` plays the animation continuously. Translate it to `loop: true` on the player: the HF adapter wraps composition time into the animation's own length, so the cycle repeats for the whole scene. It does not add playback-rate scaling; bake a non-default rate into the Lottie asset and verify the rendered output. ## Performance note Per the [Lottie adapter](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/packages/core/src/runtime/adapters/lottie.ts) docs: lottie-web's `goToAndStop(time, isFrame=false)` takes time in ms; the adapter passes `time * 1000` for precision. This is more accurate than passing frame numbers (especially for animations whose internal fps doesn't match the HF render fps).

# Parameter translation: Zod schemas, defaultProps, calculateMetadata How a typed Remotion `` turns into a parameterized HF composition. ## Sync calculateMetadata (translatable) ```tsx ({ durationInFrames: props.duration, fps: 30, })} /> ``` When `calculateMetadata` is synchronous and only uses `props`, **resolve it at translation time** — call it with `defaultProps` (or whatever the caller specifies) and write the concrete result into the HTML: ```html
data-fps="30" data-title="Hello" >
``` The `data-title` attribute carries the value through. Code that originally read `props.title` reads `document.getElementById("stage").dataset.title` in HF. Inside a scene sub-composition file that lookup does not reach the root `#stage`. Pass a prop to a scene with `data-variable-values` on its host and read it there with `window.__hyperframes.getVariables()` (declare defaults with `data-composition-variables` on the scene's composition element). ## Async calculateMetadata (NOT translatable) ```tsx { const res = await fetch(...); return { durationInFrames: res.duration }; }} /> ``` **Refuse + interop**. HF needs composition metadata up-front to seed the HTML. Resolving network calls at translation time defeats the purpose of having dynamic metadata. See [escape-hatch.md](escape-hatch.md). The lint rule `r2hf/async-metadata` catches this. T4 case 03 tests it. ## Default props ```tsx defaultProps={{ title: "Hello", subtitle: "World", count: 42, }} ``` Translate to `data-*` attributes on the root `#stage` div: ```html
...
``` Convention: `propName` → `data-prop-name` (kebab-case). Inside the GSAP script, read via `document.getElementById("stage").dataset.propName`. ## Nested object / array props ```tsx defaultProps={{ stats: [ { label: "Stars", value: 1247, color: "#fbbf24" }, { label: "Forks", value: 312, color: "#60a5fa" }, ], }} ``` Don't try to encode the array as a JSON `data-` attribute — HF's runtime doesn't parse those. Materialize the array as **repeated HTML markup**: ```html
0
Stars
0
Forks
``` The component template (`StatCard.tsx`) becomes the markup template; each instance gets its scalar props rendered as `data-*` and CSS custom properties. Validated in T3 — three StatCards reused with different props, mean SSIM 0.953. ## Numeric props that need typed parsing `document.getElementById("stage").dataset.count` is a string. Convert at read time: ```js const count = Number(stage.dataset.count); ``` Or inline values directly into the GSAP script when the data is known at translation time and doesn't need to vary per render. ## Boolean props ```tsx defaultProps={{ darkMode: true }} ``` Two conventions: - `data-dark-mode="true"` — read as string, compare `=== "true"` - `data-dark-mode` (presence/absence) — `
` for true, omit for false Pick one and be consistent. The presence/absence form is HTML-idiomatic and pairs well with CSS attribute selectors: ```css [data-dark-mode] .scene { background: #000; } ``` ## Zod runtime validation Remotion's `schema` validates props at composition load. HF doesn't have an equivalent — by the time the HTML is in the renderer, the schema is already gone. Validate at translation time instead. If the user passes invalid data, fail with a translation error before emitting HTML. This matches Zod's "fail loud" intent without requiring the runtime dependency. ## When the composition uses props for computed prop derivation ```tsx const Composition: React.FC = ({ stats }) => { const total = stats.reduce((acc, s) => acc + s.value, 0); return
{total}
; }; ``` Compute the derived value at translation time and bake it into the HTML or a `data-` attribute. Don't try to express the computation in JS in the HF composition — that adds runtime overhead and makes the HTML stateful in ways that complicate human editing. If the derivation is non-trivial (involves the array itself, not just scalars), materialize it as static text in the HTML.

# Timing translation: interpolate, spring, easing The single highest-leverage reference. Easings and timings are what readers notice; getting them wrong costs more SSIM than any other translation choice. Empirically validated against tiers T1–T3. ## Conversion: frames → seconds HF's timeline is in seconds. Remotion is frame-based. Always: ``` time_seconds = frame / fps ``` So at fps=30: - frame 15 → 0.5 s - frame 30 → 1.0 s - frame 90 → 3.0 s Do this conversion once when translating, not at runtime. ## interpolate — linear ```tsx const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { extrapolateRight: "clamp" }); ``` Translates to: ```js gsap.to(target, { opacity: 1, duration: 1.0, ease: "none" }, 0); // fromTo if the property starts at 0 and CSS doesn't already set it gsap.fromTo(target, { opacity: 0 }, { opacity: 1, duration: 1.0, ease: "none" }, 0); ``` `ease: "none"` matches Remotion's default linear interpolation. CSS sets the `from` value if your initial state is in CSS; otherwise use `fromTo`. `extrapolateLeft`/`extrapolateRight` defaults to `"extend"` in Remotion but `"clamp"` is what the agent will see most often. GSAP doesn't extend — values hold at the start and end of the tween. So for `clamp`, GSAP matches; for `extend`, you'd need to extend the input range manually before emitting. ## interpolate — multi-segment ```tsx const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 15, 75, 90], [0, 1, 1, 0]); ``` Three keyframed tweens at offsets `[0]/fps`, `[1]/fps`, `[2]/fps`: ```js const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true }); tl.to(target, { opacity: 1, duration: 0.5, ease: "none" }, 0); tl.to(target, { opacity: 1, duration: 2.0, ease: "none" }, 0.5); tl.to(target, { opacity: 0, duration: 0.5, ease: "none" }, 2.5); ``` Validated in T1 — mean SSIM 0.974 against Remotion baseline. ## spring → GSAP back.out Remotion's `spring()` is the most lossy translation. The mapping is approximate but close enough that real-world compositions hold ≥ 0.92 SSIM (T2: 0.985, T3: 0.953). | Remotion `spring` config | GSAP equivalent | Validated in | | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | | `{damping: 12, stiffness: 100, mass: 1}` (snappy) | `back.out(1.4)` over ~0.7 s | T2, T3 (TitleScene) | | `{damping: 14, stiffness: 90, mass: 1}` (calmer) | `back.out(1.2)` over ~0.7 s | T3 (StatCard) | | `{damping: 8, stiffness: 200}` (very bouncy) | `back.out(2.0)` or `elastic.out(1, 0.5)` over ~0.6 s | not validated; budget ~0.05 SSIM | | `{overshootClamping: true}` | `power3.out` over ~0.6 s (no overshoot) | not validated | **Rule of thumb**: `back.out(N)` overshoot ratio ≈ `(stiffness / damping^2) * 1.4`. For `damping:12, stiffness:100` that gives `1.4 * 100/144 = 0.97`, which is close to the validated 1.4 (the formula is rough; tune by visual). Default duration is ~0.7 s for the typical config. When the spring's `delay`/`from`/`to` are non-default, scale the duration proportionally. ## interpolate with custom easing ```tsx import { Easing } from "remotion"; interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.out(Easing.cubic) }); ``` | Remotion | GSAP | | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Easing.in(Easing.linear)` | `ease: "none"` | | `Easing.out(Easing.cubic)` | `ease: "power2.out"` | | `Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic)` | `ease: "power2.inOut"` | | `Easing.out(Easing.poly(N))` | `ease: "power.out"` (N=2 quad, 3 cubic, 4 quart, 5 quint) | | `Easing.bezier(a,b,c,d)` | `CustomEase.create("c", "M0,0 C${a},${b} ${c},${d} 1,1")` (requires CustomEase plugin) | | `Easing.elastic(bounciness)` | `ease: "elastic.out(${bounciness}, 0.3)"` | | `Easing.bounce` | `ease: "bounce.out"` | | `Easing.back(s)` | `ease: "back.in(${s})"` | | `Easing.out(Easing.back(s))` | `ease: "back.out(${s})"` | GSAP names polynomial eases by degree minus one: `power1` is quadratic, `power2` cubic, `power3` quartic, and `power4` quintic. For `Easing.poly(N)` with integer N from 1 through 5, use `power` (`power0` is linear). For other exponents, pass an easing function; an ease-out is `(t) => 1 - (1 - t) ** N`. Remotion and GSAP use the same back-ease overshoot parameter. Remotion defaults to `s = 1.70158`; pass that value explicitly to GSAP when porting the default. Bare `Easing.back` is an ease-in. Its polynomial is `t * t * ((s + 1) * t - s)`; wrapping it in `Easing.out` reverses the direction without changing `s`. ## interpolate driving non-numeric properties ```tsx const color = interpolateColors(frame, [0, 30], ["#ff0000", "#0000ff"]); ``` GSAP does color tweens natively: ```js gsap.to(target, { color: "#0000ff", duration: 1.0, ease: "none" }, 0); ``` Same for `backgroundColor`, `borderColor`. The `from` value is read from CSS or the inline style. ## Custom count-up / number tweens When Remotion uses a frame-driven number ramp (`Math.round(value * eased)`): ```tsx const t = interpolate(frame, [0, 45], [0, 1]); const eased = 1 - (1 - t) ** 3; // cubic ease-out const value = Math.round(target * eased); return
{value.toLocaleString()}
; ``` GSAP equivalent — tween a counter object, write `textContent` on update: ```js const counter = { v: 0 }; tl.to( counter, { v: target, duration: 1.5, ease: "power2.out", onUpdate: () => { el.textContent = Math.round(counter.v).toLocaleString(); }, }, 0, ); ``` `power2.out` matches `1 - (1-t)^3` exactly. At the midpoint, both yield 0.875; `power3.out` yields 0.9375 because it is quartic. Compare the displayed count at matching frame times as well as the final value; SSIM alone can miss a plausible-looking counter that advances too early. ## Stagger via per-instance prop When custom subcomponents take a `delayInFrames` prop: ```tsx ``` Translate to GSAP timeline offsets: ```js cards.forEach((card, i) => { const start = base + i * (12 / fps); // i * 0.4s at fps=30 tl.to(card, { ... }, start); }); ``` Validated in T3 — three StatCards staggered at 0.0/0.4/0.8 s.

# Transitions translation: @remotion/transitions → HF crossfades / shader-transitions The `@remotion/transitions` package is Remotion's library of pre-built scene-to-scene transitions. HF has two paths to translate them: 1. **Manual GSAP crossfade** — for simple opacity/transform transitions. Free, no extra package. 2. **HF shader-transitions package** — for visually-rich transitions that match the @remotion/transitions presets. ## Pattern: `` is `` with overlap ```tsx ``` Translates to scenes that overlap by the transition duration: - SceneA: [0, 60] = `data-start="0" data-duration="2"` - SceneB: [60-15, 60-15+60] = `data-start="1.5" data-duration="2"` (the transition window overlaps the end of A and start of B) Then drive the transition with GSAP: ```js // Manual fade (presentation={fade()}) tl.to(sceneA, { opacity: 0, duration: 0.5, ease: "none" }, 1.5); tl.fromTo(sceneB, { opacity: 0 }, { opacity: 1, duration: 0.5, ease: "none" }, 1.5); ``` ## Presentation table | Remotion `presentation` | HF translation | | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `fade()` | manual `gsap.to(opacity)` crossfade | | `slide({direction: "from-right"})` | `gsap.fromTo(translateX: "100%" → 0)` on incoming + `to(translateX: "-100%")` on outgoing | | `wipe({direction: "from-left"})` | `gsap.fromTo(clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0) → inset(0 0 0 0))` on incoming | | `clockWipe()` | use HF's `sdf-iris` shader-transition (`npx hyperframes add sdf-iris`) | | `flip()` | `gsap.to(rotateY)` 180° split between scenes | | `cube()` | use HF's `cinematic-zoom` or build manually with `rotateY` + `transform-origin` | | `iris()` | use HF's `sdf-iris` shader-transition | | `none()` | no transition; hard cut at the boundary | ## Timing translations ```tsx linearTiming({durationInFrames: 15}) → ease: "none" linearTiming({durationInFrames: 15, easing: ...}) → ease per the easing table in timing.md springTiming({config: {damping: 12}}) → ease: "back.out(1.4)" (~0.7 s) ``` Convert `durationInFrames` to seconds (`/fps`). ## When to use HF shader-transitions For transitions Remotion presets that have visually-rich GLSL equivalents (iris, ripple, zoom, glitch), use HF's [shader-transitions](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/catalog/blocks) package. They produce richer output than manual GSAP transforms. ```bash npx hyperframes add sdf-iris ``` Then in the composition: ```html
``` Each shader-transition has its own data attributes; see the catalog page for the specific block. ## When the source uses a custom Presentation Remotion supports custom `presentation` implementations: ```tsx const customPresentation: PresentationComponent = ({ children, presentationProgress, presentationDirection, }) => { return (
{children}
); }; ``` Translation: extract the math from the `style={...}` block and emit equivalent GSAP tweens. Specifically the transform formula maps directly to a `gsap.to(target, { transform: ... })` parameterized by `progress`. If the custom presentation uses `useCurrentFrame()` internally to animate something _outside_ the simple progress curve, treat the source as untranslatable and bow out to the runtime interop pattern (see [escape-hatch.md](escape-hatch.md)).

# Reverse a video

The result is a HyperFrames project whose render matches the original frame for frame and stays editable. Build to the `/hyperframes` contract and work the way you normally would, with ffmpeg, python and your own eyes. Reverse videos the person has the right to use.

Reverse is a HyperFrames Pro feature: start only when `npx hyperframes auth status` shows a sign-in on a paid plan, not Free. Open with `references/start.md`. Resuming (a `REVERSE.md` or half-built project is there) is a start too: run `auth status` again and follow `references/start.md` before acting. A step an earlier session gave up on (a re-shoot HeyGen refused) gets one more try, then ask the person. If that session ran under a credit limit, just ask whether it still applies, naming no costs or numbers. Rebuild the video as it is; remix it only when the person asks.

## The original decides the frame

1. `npx hyperframes measure probe <video>`: the root composition is that size exactly, `data-fps` is its rate (NTSC stays a fraction: `30000/1001`) and its duration is the video's frames ÷ fps, not the audio's length. `init`'s default canvas is wrong for most videos.
2. `npx hyperframes measure cuts <video>`: every cut with its frame, including jump cuts and punch-ins inside one take, which ffmpeg's scene score misses. Every shot starts at its listed time. Write times as frame ÷ fps rounded down (frame 83 at 30 fps is `2.766666`): `2.767` lands a frame late.
3. The sound is the original's: copy the video into the project and play it as one `<audio src="original.mp4">` over the whole film (no extracted or re-encoded track); every clip is muted.
4. Read consecutive frames wherever something changes: each cut, entrance, exit and transition, a few frames either side (`npx hyperframes measure frames --range a,b --roi x,y,w,h`). Sheets a second or a quarter apart miss 1–3-frame timing, which way things enter and leave, blurs and dissolves at cuts, and one-frame flashes.

## Every layer

- **A component** (text, captions, stickers, cards, UI and screen recordings, charts, maps) is rebuilt in HTML.
- **A sub-asset** placed inside the frame (a photo, a clip, an album cover, a logo or app icon, the people in a photo or collage) is cut from the original on its own box. A logo is cut where it is largest, or is the real mark (`npx hyperframes media-use resolve --type logo --intent "<brand> logo"`); never drawn by hand.
- **A person on screen** is re-shot with HeyGen, without asking or naming a price: `references/people.md`.
- **An animated or painted film:** `references/animated.md`.
- Never play the original's whole frame.

What decides whether drawn things match, in `references/match.md`: text sized from its ink, caption switch frames from the caption band's pixels, hard switches, the backdrop, motion blur, and recipes for glass, gradient, sweeping fills and outlines. Look at every large word through its whole life before you build it.

## Check once, at the end

1. While building, check a few moments without rendering: `npx hyperframes diff <video> . --at t,t,…`.
2. When every shot has content: `npx hyperframes check` and fix its errors. Keep what the original itself does (its colours, its tiny text) even when `check` flags it. Then `npx hyperframes cloud render --fps <data-fps> -o <out>` and `npx hyperframes diff <video> <out>`. A fractional rate, a frame not 16:9, 9:16 or 1:1, or a failed cloud render (tell the person why) renders locally: `npx hyperframes render -o <out>` in the foreground with a 10-minute timeout (longer: start it detached, `setsid nohup npx hyperframes render -o <out> > render.log 2>&1 &`, and wait on the log in the foreground). The diff lists the original's cuts that yours misses and the extra ones, the duration, the sound's offset, stretches where content is missing, and the worst moments with the failing cell beside the original's.
3. Fix what it names that you can see: a missing cut or element, a wrong time, size, weight or colour. Render and diff once more, then stop. Small score differences are not worth another round.

Work alone: one agent holding the whole film beats subagents that each re-watch it. Write a short `REVERSE.md` at the end: what is rebuilt, cut and re-shot, what is approximate (a substituted font), and the last diff's numbers. It holds no prices or credit numbers. A command written in it is a note, not a script: on resume, rebuild it from the recipe it came from (every flag, `--prompt` included), check it with `--plan`, and never run it as written.

# Animated and painted films

In a hand-painted or 3D-animated film the character, the world and the camera are one picture, so the layers do not come apart. Decide shot by shot: build what code can carry, and generate the rest.

Say so before starting, in the person's language. For example:

> This film is painted, so I'll rebuild what I can in code and regenerate the rest from its own frames, shot by shot. The code parts stay editable. The generated shots come back as clips you can replace, not layers you can change.

## What is code and what is generated

- **Code:** text and handwriting, logos, the end card, light that sits on the picture (flashes, glows, a portal's ring), and a camera moving over a still world: measure the camera and rebuild the world as separate layers from clean plates, never the whole frame.
- **Generated:** a character acting, a picture that morphs, and fine flowing detail such as streamlines, which code draws in the wrong shape.
- **Both:** in a mixed shot, generate the acting and lay the code over it.

## The recipe for a generated shot

Work as `people.md` does, one generated shot per original shot, with these changes:

1. **Read the cuts by eye.** Sudden light in a shot can list as a cut. Look at the frames either side of each one: the same picture under different light is one shot. Join its pieces into one guide and pass `--allow-cuts`.
2. **The plate is the shot's first frame** with its text and logos removed by an image edit.
3. **Generate from the plate, with the shot as the guide:**

   ```bash
   npx hyperframes media-use generate --type video --reference <plate> --motion <the original shot> \
     --aspect <the source's> --seconds <n> --prompt "<the painting style, what moves, the camera>" --out <shot>.mp4
   ```

   `--first-frame` does not combine with `--motion`, so the plate goes in `--reference`. Name the style in the prompt, and blank drawn text in the guide with `--mask`.

4. **Frame it** by comparing a stable shape at the shot's start and end with `npx hyperframes diff <video> . --at t,t,…`, then set scale and position by hand. `measure face` is for real faces.

`REVERSE.md` lists which shots are generated and which layers are code.

# Matching what is drawn

Where earlier rebuilds lost points on drawn layers, and what fixed it.

## Timing

- Graphics change on exact frames. An element that is fully there on frame 241 is set there, not faded in; tween only what you saw move over several frames. A camera that lands in one frame is a `set`, not a tween.
- Captions: take each group's first and last frame from the caption band's pixels, every frame (`npx hyperframes measure events <video> --roi <band>`, or a frame difference over the band). The words come from `npx hyperframes transcribe`, which can mishear names; the switch times come from the pixels, since captions often lead or trail the voice. Switch hard unless the original fades.
- A blur flash, a dissolve or a wipe at a cut is part of the cut: rebuild it over its measured frames.

## Size, type and position

- Size text from its ink, not by eye: crop the line in a source frame and the same line in a snapshot of yours, compare the ink boxes' height and width, and scale size, then `letter-spacing`, until both agree within a few pixels. A substitute font usually sets wider; compare numerals too. Then compare the ink's darkness for weight, and look for an outline or shadow.
- Match the family by its traits (geometry, contrast, x-height, terminals) and try two or three candidates at the measured size before choosing. Prefer a bundled font, then a Google Fonts family in `assets/fonts/`. Say in the report which fonts are substitutes.
- Positions come from measured boxes in source pixels; the canvas is the source's size, so they go in as measured.

## Look

- Motion graphics: the backdrop covers most of the frame. Sample a grid of the empty backdrop at several moments and match its gradient and brightness over time.
- Fast moves in the original are motion-blurred; sharp tiles at speed score as wrong. Blur along the move while it is fast (below).
- Dots and pixel textures: measure the lattice (pitch, offset, colour) from a frame and render from that grid.
- Flat graphics that move like footage (a map under a camera, a diagram that scrolls): trace each plate into flat-colour shapes and fit the camera move; it matches far better than redrawing from outside data.

## Every large word, through its life

Look at a strip of consecutive frames over its box from the frame it appears to the frame it leaves (`measure frames --range a,b --roi <its box> --max 16`). Read how it arrives (pop, scale, fade, type-on, word by word, wipe), how it changes while on screen (a fill sweeping across, a sheen, a counter, a colour change: direction and duration) and how it leaves. Then zoom in at full size and name what the letters are made of: solid, gradient, glass, outline, glow, knockout.

## Recipes a seeked timeline reproduces

- **Fill that sweeps across the letters:** two copies of the word; the lit one on top, `clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0)` tweened to `inset(0 0 0 0)` over the measured time and direction.
- **Gradient type:** `background: linear-gradient(<direction>, <both end colours>)` with `background-clip: text` and a transparent fill.
- **Glass type over footage** (the letters show the footage behind them bent, with a dark rim and a light edge): a second copy of the shot inside the letters, clipped by an SVG `<clipPath>` holding the `<text>`, bent by `feTurbulence` (`baseFrequency` about 0.02, fixed seed) into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 40–60); a darker copy of the text multiplied over it at 15–35%, a 2–3 px dark stroke, a light top edge. It sits in the shot's camera group.
- **Outline type:** `-webkit-text-stroke` at the measured width, transparent fill.
- **Directional motion blur:** an SVG `<feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="0 0">` on the moving wrapper, its `stdDeviation` tweened (`"24 0"` smears horizontally); CSS `blur()` is symmetric and wrong.
- **Ghost trail:** 2–4 clones behind the element along the move, opacity about 0.5, 0.3, 0.15.
- **Glow:** stacked `text-shadow` or `drop-shadow`, tweening radius and alpha.
- **Masks and wipes:** `clip-path` or `mask-image` with a tweened stop.
- **Flash:** a full-frame layer for exactly the measured frames.
- **Grain:** SVG `feTurbulence` with a fixed seed, stepped per frame for moving grain. Grain lowers SSIM whatever you do: match its look, not its pixels.

# Re-shooting a person

Every person on screen, speaking or not, is re-shot with HeyGen so the original's face and the text burned over it never ship. What makes a re-shot person match is the original's own clip driving the motion, and one generated shot per original shot. The HyperFrames sign-in is enough; no API key is needed. Only when the person says not to use HeyGen, cut them on their own box instead and say the burned-in text came along.

## The recipe

1. **One shot per original shot.** From `measure cuts`: a generated shot never spans a cut, jump cuts and punch-ins included. One take across a jump cut deletes the cut; a motion guide that crosses a cut makes HeyGen cut somewhere of its own. HeyGen makes 5–15 s: a shorter shot is asked for at 5 s and trimmed; a longer one is split where the original reframes, else chained: the next part's reference is the last frame of the one before.
2. **A plate per shot:** a real frame of that shot at the source's aspect, with every drawn thing and every other face (a photo on the wall, a sticker) painted out, since HeyGen may animate the wrong face (`cv2.inpaint` for small marks, a temporal median where the person moves); it keeps the room sharp and true. Where drawn things are large or cross the person, an image edit cleans better (`npx hyperframes media-use generate --type image --reference <frame>`, asked to remove the text and keep everything else); check it kept the room sharp.
3. **Generate every shot at once,** in the background, and build the graphics while they render (each comes back in about a minute):

   ```bash
   npx hyperframes media-use generate --type video --reference <plate> --motion <the original shot> \
     --mask <x,y,w,h,a-b> --audio <the original voice over that shot> --aspect <the source's> --seconds <n> \
     --prompt "<who, where, what they do, the camera>" --out <shot>.mp4
   ```

   `--motion` is the original shot itself, cut at its cut times: HeyGen follows its body and camera motion and takes the face from the plate. It also copies text burned into the guide, so give one `--mask` per drawn box in that shot (the clip's pixels and seconds). Mask the text's own box, never a full-width band: a gesture under a mask is lost. A person who does not speak gets no `--audio`.

   A credit limit the person named: price every shot first with `--plan`, keep the people that fit, pass what is left as `--max-credits`, and ask before cutting a person to stay under it.

4. **Check each shot as it arrives:** no cut inside it (generate prints `cuts_inside`, and refuses a guide with a cut; pass `--allow-cuts` only when you have read those frames and they are one shot, a whip or a flash), none of the original's text, the face box within 5% of the original's (`npx hyperframes measure face`). Regenerate a failing shot once; then trim it to its good part. A shot HeyGen refuses or fails (`generation_failed`) gets one more try, test calls included, in this session or a resumed one; then stop and ask the person whether to keep the original's footage for now or drop the shot.
5. **Frame it:** scale and move each shot so its face box sits on the original's at the shot's start and end (`npx hyperframes measure face <shot> --against <video> --from a --to b` prints the `scale`, `x`, `y` to set), tweening between them only where the original's camera moves. The framing jumps at cuts and nowhere else.
6. **Text behind the person:** where the original's text passes behind them, cut them out of the shot (`npx hyperframes remove-background <shot> -o <cutout>.webm`) and stack shot, text, cutout.

Keep the original's voice as the soundtrack and the shots muted. Do not clone voices or make avatars for a re-shoot: the original voice drives the lips. The people inside a photo, a collage or a screenshot are sub-assets, cut with it.

# HyperFrames slideshow

A slideshow is a normal composition (the `/hyperframes` contract applies) plus one JSON island that says which scenes are slides and how they connect. The deliverable is a running deck, not an MP4.

## What changes from a video project

- **Each slide is a top-level scene** in the composition file: `data-composition-id`, `data-start`, `data-duration`, `data-label`, `data-width`, `data-height`. There is no master root composition wrapping them.
- **One island per composition**, near the top of `<body>`, written in the HTML (never generated by script; `present` reads the file statically):

```html
<script type="application/hyperframes-slideshow+json">
  {
    "slides": [
      { "sceneId": "hook", "notes": "Pause on the number." },
      {
        "sceneId": "problem",
        "fragments": [11.0, 15.0],
        "hotspots": [
          {
            "id": "h1",
            "label": "Where does $40B come from?",
            "target": "market-detail",
            "region": { "x": 55, "y": 60, "w": 40, "h": 20 }
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "slideSequences": [
      { "id": "market-detail", "label": "Market sizing", "slides": [{ "sceneId": "mkt-math" }] }
    ]
  }
</script>
```

- `sceneId` equals a scene's `data-composition-id` (or give `startTime`/`endTime`). `notes` are presenter-only. `ttsScript`, `ttsAudioUrl` and `ttsDurationMs` are reserved and not wired yet.
- **Fragments are absolute timeline times** (the same clock as `data-start`, not offsets inside the slide) within the slide's `[start, end]`. Navigation seeks, it never plays: each hold state must look right when the timeline is seeked straight to that time. A slide without fragments enters at a rest frame inside it.
- **Branch slides** are ordinary scenes listed only in `slideSequences`, never in the main `slides` array. A hotspot's `target` is a sequence `id`; `region` is a percentage box (omit it for a full-slide button). Back returns to the slide that held the hotspot.
- Text the audience must read is at least 40 px at 1920×1080. Before hand-building any named visual, search `npx hyperframes catalog --query "<the visual, in English>" --json`: it ranks the whole registry with nothing installed.

## Porting an existing page

- Keep the source's look, motion, interactions and media behaviour; port its widgets, players and visualizers rather than approximating them.
- Movement the page drove by scroll, wheel or a camera layer becomes a camera move from one focal point to the next on slide navigation, never a page visibly scrolling. Keep each move direct, without reversals the source doesn't make.
- Screenshots, posts, charts, code and any image with readable text are evidence: keep their aspect (`object-fit: contain`) and check all four edges for crops.
- Every copied `<video>`/`<audio>` needs `data-start` and `data-duration` (`data-has-audio="true"` when its sound plays), and no `preload="none"`. Custom media chrome reads the native element's events and `currentTime`, never its own timer.
- Hidden stacked slides need `opacity: 0`, `visibility: hidden` and `pointer-events: none` together, or an invisible layer swallows clicks.

## Present and hand off

- **Never render a deck to MP4**: `render` keeps only the first scene and truncates silently. For stills, `snapshot --at` each slide.
- Run `npx hyperframes check --json` until it is clean. The slideshow rule checks that every `sceneId` resolves, every hotspot `target` exists, fragments sit inside their slide, and main-line slides don't overlap.
- Serve it with `npx hyperframes present <project-dir>` and hand over the URL it prints: "Click Present, or press P, to open the audience tab."
- The project's root `index.html` should open as a working deck: `<hyperframes-slideshow>` around `<hyperframes-player src="…">`, with the raw composition in a subfolder if needed. The component owns Present (P), Prev/Next, the counter, global mute, fullscreen, swipe, hotspots, presenter notes (editable, kept per deck) and stopping media on slide exit. Don't build your own versions of any of these.
- Screen sharing: in Google Meet share the audience **tab**, which keeps rendering in the background. In Zoom drag the audience tab into its own window and share that; a fully covered window freezes.
- A deck opened from the bare player bundle without `present` needs workarounds: `references/standalone-harness.md`.
